mainTopic: Decrees on יחוד, the laws of the king (horses, wealth, wives and his ספר תורה), lessons from שלמה, and the change of the Torah's script under עזרא
overview: The amud opens by finishing רב's statement that after the story of אמנון and תמר, דוד's court made a decree. The גמרא points out that יחוד with forbidden relatives is already a Torah law, so it rereads the decree as being about יחוד with an unmarried woman. Next it brings רב's teachings about אדוניה, who tried to make himself king. A new משנה then lists limits on a מלך: he may not have too many horses or too much silver and gold, and he must keep his own ספר תורה with him. The גמרא explains how the word 'לו' shapes each of these limits. The two limits on horses and wealth allow what the army needs, and the limit on wives applies only to the king. רבי יצחק discusses פסוקים about שלמה's horses and silver, and teaches that the Torah hides its reasons because even שלמה stumbled when they were revealed. רבא teaches that every Jew must write his own ספר תורה, and a king writes two. The amud ends with how the Torah's script changed in עזרא's time, and with רבי יוסי's praise of עזרא, whose proof פסוק comes on the next amud.

steps.title: The decrees about seclusion and the unmarried woman
steps.stepSummary: רב's statement ends: after the episode of אמנון and תמר, they decreed about יחוד and about a פנויה.
steps.simpleTranslation: They made decrees about a man being alone with a woman, and about an unmarried woman.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a statement of רב that began just before this point. He said that after what happened with אמנון and תמר, the court made new decrees, and here we learn what they were.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The decrees named are about יחוד (being alone together) and about a פנויה (an unmarried woman). This sets up the next step, where the גמרא asks how יחוד could be a new decree at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Seclusion; a man and a woman being alone together in private
They decreed; the חכמים made a protective rule

phrases.english: About seclusion, and about the unmarried woman.
phrases.notes: This finishes רב's statement from just before: after the story of אמנון and תמר, the court made decrees about these two things.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the statement of רב that began before this section
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After the episode of אמנון and תמר, the court decreed about יחוד and about a פנויה.

steps.title: But seclusion is already forbidden by the Torah
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how יחוד could be a rabbinic decree when it is already forbidden by the Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: Seclusion? That is already a Torah law!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב: a decree is something new the חכמים add, but יחוד is already forbidden by the Torah itself. The next step brings the source for this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A decree only makes sense for something the Torah has not already forbidden. If יחוד is דאורייתא, then saying דוד's court decreed against it seems wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: From the Torah; a Torah-level law, not a rabbinic one

phrases.english: Seclusion? It is from the Torah!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the claim in step 1 that יחוד was a new decree
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's claim that דוד's court decreed against יחוד
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: You cannot make a rabbinic decree against something the Torah already forbids, and יחוד is forbidden by the Torah.

steps.title: The Torah hint for the prohibition of seclusion
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי שמעון בן יהוצדק, finds a hint for יחוד in the פסוק about a brother who entices to idolatry.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יהוצדק: Where is the Torah hint for seclusion? The פסוק says, 'If your brother, the son of your mother, entices you.' Does only a mother's son entice, and not a father's son? Rather, the Torah is teaching that a son may be alone with his mother, but nobody else may be alone with any of the women the Torah forbids to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its challenge by bringing a source showing that יחוד is forbidden by the Torah. It reads an unusual detail in a פסוק as a hint to this law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says 'son of your mother' when a brother from the father is just as likely to entice. The answer is that brothers from the same mother grow close, because a son may be alone with his own mother and so is often at home with her. A stepmother is an ערוה, so a son cannot be alone with her, and brothers from the same father spend less time together.

keyTerms.meaning: A hint; a source that suggests a law without stating it outright
One who entices another to worship idols
Women forbidden to a man because of close family relation
Is secluded; is alone in private with someone

steps.confusionAlert: The פסוק is not saying that only a mother's son can entice. The גמרא reads the extra words 'son of your mother' as a hint about who may be alone with whom.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יְהוֹצָדָק:
phrases.english: As Rabbi Yoḥanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak:
From where is there a hint for seclusion in the Torah?
As it is said: “If your brother, the son of your mother, entices you.”
But does only a mother's son entice,
and a father's son does not entice?
Rather, it comes to tell you:
A son may be alone with his mother,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין אַחֵר מִתְיַיחֵד עִם כׇּל עֲרָיוֹת שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה.
phrases.english: but no one else may be alone with any of the women forbidden in the Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יְהוֹצָדָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source that supports the challenge in step 2
steps.raayaObject: That יחוד with עריות is forbidden by the Torah
steps.raayaSupportSource: The פסוק 'כי יסיתך אחיך בן אמך' (דברים 13:7), read as a hint, from רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי שמעון בן יהוצדק

steps.title: The decree was about seclusion with an unmarried woman
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads רב: the decree was against יחוד with a פנויה, which the Torah did not already forbid.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: they decreed against seclusion with an unmarried woman.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by changing how we read רב's words. The two items in step 1 become one decree: no יחוד with an unmarried woman.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah forbids יחוד only with עריות. An unmarried woman who is not a relative is not an ערוה, so being alone with her was not forbidden by the Torah. דוד's court added that as a new decree, which fits what happened with אמנון and תמר.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, say; the גמרא changes how a statement should be read

steps.whatToRemember: יחוד with עריות is forbidden by the Torah. יחוד with an unmarried woman is a rabbinic decree from the time of דוד.

phrases.english: Rather, say:
They decreed against seclusion with an unmarried woman.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אֵימָא: גָּזְרוּ עַל יִיחוּד דִּפְנוּיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 2 and 3
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the wording of the earlier statement
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב meant a decree against יחוד in general, which would clash with the Torah prohibition
steps.terutzMaskana: רב meant a new decree against יחוד with a פנויה, which the Torah had not forbidden

steps.title: אדוניה tried to make the kingship fit him
steps.stepSummary: Moving to another son of דוד, רב teaches that אדוניה tried to make the kingship fit him, but it did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: “And אדוניה son of חגית raised himself up, saying: I will be king.” רב יהודה said in the name of רב: This teaches that he tried to make it fit him, but it did not fit him.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the גמרא was just talking about אמנון, a son of דוד, it now opens a new topic about another son, אדוניה. רב explains what the word 'raised himself up' in the פסוק is hinting at.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word מתנשא suggests that אדוניה tried to take on kingship for himself. רב learns from it that he tried to make the kingship suit him, but it did not suit him, because he was not meant to be king.

keyTerms.meaning: It teaches; introduces a lesson learned from a פסוק
To fit him; to suit him

phrases.english: “And Adonijah son of Haggith raised himself up, saying:
I will be king.”
Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
This teaches that he tried to make it fit him,
but it did not fit him.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַאֲדֹנִיָּה בֶן חַגִּית מִתְנַשֵּׂא לֵאמֹר אֲנִי אֶמְלֹךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the topic of אמנון to another son of דוד, אדוניה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The word מתנשא teaches that אדוניה tried to make the kingship fit him, but it did not fit him.

steps.title: What was special about the runners of אדוניה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the פסוק about אדוניה's chariots and fifty runners and asks what was unusual about that.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'He made himself chariots and riders and fifty men to run before him.' What is so special about that?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues with אדוניה and quotes the פסוק about his chariots and runners. It asks what is new here, and this sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Many wealthy people kept chariots and runners, so the פסוק would not seem to be telling us anything unusual. The גמרא assumes the פסוק must be pointing to something special about these runners.

keyTerms.meaning: Something new or special; a point worth teaching
Runners who go ahead of a king or prince

phrases.english: "And he made himself chariots and riders
phrases.notes: מלכים א 1:5. This is about אדוניה, from the previous step.

phrases.english: and fifty men running before him."
What is special about this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the discussion of אדוניה by looking at the next words of the פסוק.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What was unusual about אדוניה's runners that made the פסוק mention them.

steps.title: The runners had their spleens removed and their feet hollowed
steps.stepSummary: רב explains that all of אדוניה's runners had been physically changed so they could run faster.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: All of them had their spleens removed and the soles of their feet hollowed out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by saying that these were no ordinary runners. Their bodies had been altered so they would run faster.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The special point is not that אדוניה had runners, but the unusual way they were prepared. This fits the picture from step 5 of אדוניה trying hard to look like a king.

keyTerms.meaning: People whose soles were hollowed out

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
All of them had their spleens removed
and had the soles of their feet hollowed out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of what was special about the runners.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The runners had their spleens removed and the soles of their feet hollowed out, which made them unusually fast.

steps.title: משנה: limits on a king's horses and money
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה rules that a king may keep horses only for his chariots, and silver and gold only for supplying his army.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He shall not have many horses', except what he needs for his chariot. 'He shall not have very much silver and gold', except enough to pay and supply his soldiers.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It takes two Torah limits on a king and explains what he is still allowed to have.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah's limits are not total bans. The king may have what he needs to do his job, meaning horses for his chariots and money for his army. Only extra beyond that is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: He shall not have too many; the Torah's limit on a king

phrases.english: MISHNA: "He shall not accumulate many horses for himself"
but only enough for his chariot.
"Neither shall he greatly accumulate silver and gold for himself"
but only enough to provide for his soldiers.
phrases.notes: אפסניא is a borrowed word meaning food and pay for the army.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא יַרְבֶּה לּוֹ סוּסִים אֶלָּא כְּדֵי מֶרְכַּבְתּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה. The story about אדוניה is finished.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A king may keep horses only for his chariots, and silver and gold only for supplying his army.

steps.title: משנה: the king's ספר תורה goes everywhere with him
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that the king writes a ספר תורה for himself and keeps it with him at war, in judgment, and at meals.
steps.simpleTranslation: He writes a ספר תורה for himself. When he goes out to war, he takes it with him. When he comes back, he brings it back with him. When he judges, it is with him. When he sits down to eat, it is in front of him. As the פסוק says: 'It shall be with him and he shall read in it all the days of his life.'
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with another rule for a king: his own ספר תורה must always be with him. It brings a פסוק as the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The list covers the main parts of a king's life: war, judging, and eating. The words 'with him' and 'all the days of his life' in the פסוק show that the ספר תורה is meant to be with him all the time.

keyTerms.meaning: For his own sake; his personal scroll

steps.whatToRemember: A king's limits are about not having too much for himself, and his personal ספר תורה must be with him everywhere.

phrases.english: And he writes himself a Torah scroll for his own sake.
When he goes out to war, he takes it out with him;
when he comes back in, he brings it in with him;
when he sits in judgment, it is with him;
when he reclines to eat, it is in front of him,
as it is stated: "And it shall be with him
and he shall read in it all the days of his life."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same משנה with another rule for the king.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The king writes his own ספר תורה and keeps it with him at all times, based on 'it shall be with him all the days of his life'.

steps.title: ברייתא: horses for his chariots and riders are allowed
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא learns from the word 'לו' that the ban covers horses for the king's own pleasure, not horses for his chariots and riders.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: 'He shall not have many horses for himself.' You might think he may not have even enough for his chariot and riders. So the פסוק says 'for himself': for himself he may not have many, but he may have enough for his chariots and riders.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that shows where the משנה's exception for chariot horses comes from. It reads the word 'לו', 'for himself', closely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without the word 'לו', we might think every extra horse is banned, even ones the army needs. 'לו' narrows the ban to horses kept for the king's own sake. This is the source for the משנה's 'אלא כדי מרכבתו'.

keyTerms.meaning: One might think; introduces a wrong first assumption
The פסוק teaches; brings the word that corrects the assumption

phrases.english: GEMARA: The Rabbis taught:
"He shall not accumulate many horses for himself":
Might one think, not even enough for his chariot and riders?
The verse says "for himself":
for himself he may not accumulate,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל מַרְבֶּה הוּא כְּדֵי רִכְבּוֹ וּפָרָשָׁיו.
phrases.english: but he may accumulate enough for his chariots and riders.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן לֹא יַרְבֶּה לוֹ סוּסִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source from the פסוק for the משנה's rule that chariot horses are allowed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The word 'לו' limits the ban to horses kept for the king's own sake. Horses for chariots and riders are allowed.

steps.title: Which horses does the ban cover? Idle horses
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks what 'horses' in the ban refers to, and answers: horses that are idle.
steps.simpleTranslation: So how do I explain the word 'horses' in the ban? It means idle horses.
steps.whatsHappening: Since working horses are allowed, the ברייתא asks which horses are still forbidden. It answers right away: horses that do no work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once chariot horses are allowed, the ban still needs something to apply to. The ברייתא defines that as idle horses, which serve no real purpose.

keyTerms.meaning: How do I explain or apply this word?
Idle horses that do no work

phrases.english: So how do I explain "horses"?
Idle horses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After allowing working horses, it defines which horses the ban still covers.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the word 'horses' in the ban refers to, now that chariot horses are allowed.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Idle horses that serve no working purpose.

steps.title: Even one idle horse is included in the ban
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא proves from the singular word 'סוס' that even a single idle horse is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do we know that even one idle horse falls under 'he shall not accumulate'? The פסוק says: 'in order to accumulate horse', using the singular.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks whether even one idle horse is forbidden. It proves the answer is yes from a second word in the same פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plural 'סוסים' might suggest only many horses are banned. The later words 'למען הרבות סוס' use the singular, which shows that even one idle horse counts.

phrases.english: From where do we know that even one horse
that is idle
is included in "he shall not accumulate"?
The verse says: "in order to accumulate horse."
phrases.notes: Same פסוק, דברים 17:16. Here the word סוס is singular.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִנַּיִין שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ סוּס אֶחָד וְהוּא בָּטֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the ban on idle horses down to even a single horse.
steps.raayaObject: That even one idle horse is forbidden.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The singular word 'סוס' in 'למען הרבות סוס' (דברים 17:16).

steps.title: Then why does the פסוק say 'horses' in the plural?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if one idle horse is already forbidden, why does the פסוק use the plural 'סוסים'?
steps.simpleTranslation: But if even one idle horse is already under 'he shall not accumulate', why do I need the plural 'horses'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording of the פסוק. If the singular already teaches the ban, the plural seems extra.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא assumes no word in the Torah is wasted. Once 'סוס' covers even one horse, the plural 'סוסים' must be there to teach something more.

keyTerms.meaning: But since; introduces a challenge built on what was just said
Why do I need it? Asks why a word is needed

phrases.english: But since even one horse
that is idle is included in "he shall not accumulate,"
why do I need "horses"?
phrases.notes: He means the plural word סוסים at the start of the פסוק.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מֵאַחַר דַּאֲפִילּוּ סוּס אֶחָד וְהוּא בָּטֵל קָאֵי בְּלֹא יַרְבֶּה סוּסִים לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of the פסוק based on the conclusion of the previous step.
steps.kashyaTarget: The plural word 'סוסים' in the פסוק.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the singular 'סוס' already forbids even one idle horse, the plural seems to add nothing.

steps.title: A separate לאו for each idle horse
steps.stepSummary: The plural teaches that the king breaks the לאו once for every single idle horse he keeps.
steps.simpleTranslation: It teaches that he transgresses the negative commandment for each and every horse.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the plural word teaches how many times the king sins: once for each extra horse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The singular 'סוס' tells us that even one idle horse is forbidden. The plural 'סוסים' adds that the sins add up, so each additional idle horse is another separate violation.

keyTerms.meaning: For each and every horse; counted separately

steps.whatToRemember: From the פסוק: 'לו' allows chariot horses, 'סוס' forbids even one idle horse, and 'סוסים' makes each idle horse a separate לאו.

phrases.english: To transgress a negative commandment
for each and every horse.

steps.triggerLanguage: לַעֲבוֹר בְּלֹא תַעֲשֶׂה עַל כׇּל סוּס וְסוּס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by giving the plural its own lesson.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the extra word its own separate teaching.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The plural 'סוסים' seemed extra, since the singular already covers one horse.
steps.terutzMaskana: The plural teaches that each idle horse is a separate violation of the לאו.

steps.title: Would the king be banned from army horses without the word 'for himself'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא. It sounds like only the word 'לוֹ' permits horses for chariots and riders, but a king obviously needs an army.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is the only reason the king may keep army horses that the Torah wrote 'for himself'? Without that word, would we really have said that even horses for his chariots and riders are forbidden?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the ברייתא from Step 10. It finds it strange that we needed a special word just to allow the king an army.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא used 'לוֹ' to permit horses for chariots and riders. That suggests that without 'לוֹ', even an army would be forbidden. That makes no sense, since a king must be able to defend the country, so why would the Torah need a word to tell us this?

keyTerms.meaning: The Merciful One, meaning the Torah
I would have said (what we would have thought)
His chariots and his riders (his army)

phrases.english: The reason is that the Merciful One wrote "for himself";
but if not for this, I would have said

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ כְּדֵי רִכְבּוֹ וּפָרָשָׁיו נָמֵי לָא?
phrases.english: that even enough for his chariots and riders is also not allowed?

steps.triggerLanguage: טַעְמָא דִּכְתַב רַחֲמָנָא ״לוֹ״, הָא לָאו הָכִי הֲוָה אָמֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the ברייתא's use of 'לוֹ' in Step 10 and questions why it was needed.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's claim that 'לוֹ' is what permits horses for chariots and riders.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A king's army is obviously allowed, so a word in the פסוק is not needed to permit it. The derivation seems pointless.

steps.title: 'For himself' lets the king add extra army horses
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that 'לוֹ' is not needed for the basic army. It is needed to allow the king to keep even more horses than the bare minimum.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the word is needed to allow him to add more.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The word 'לוֹ' gives the king room to keep extra horses for his army.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees the king may have the horses his army needs. 'לוֹ' teaches something extra: only horses for his personal pleasure are banned, so he may keep a generous number for the army. That means he is not limited to the strict minimum.

keyTerms.meaning: No, it is needed (for something else)

phrases.english: No, it is needed to allow adding more.
phrases.notes: He means extra horses for the army, beyond what is strictly needed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframes what the word teaches: not the basic permission, but an extra allowance.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without 'לוֹ', the king could have only the exact number of horses his army needs.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because of 'לוֹ', only personal-pleasure horses are banned, so the king may add extra horses for the army.

steps.title: The משנה's rule on silver and gold
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה: the king may not pile up silver and gold, except enough to pay for his army.
steps.simpleTranslation: "And silver and gold he shall not greatly accumulate for himself," except enough to provide for the soldiers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next ban in the משנה, about silver and gold. This line sets up the ברייתא that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same pattern as horses is starting again. The king's wealth is limited, but money for the army is not counted as forbidden accumulation.

keyTerms.meaning: He shall not accumulate a lot

phrases.english: "And silver and gold he shall not greatly accumulate for himself,"
phrases.notes: דברים 17:17. The גמרא is quoting our משנה here.

phrases.english: except for enough to provide the soldiers' upkeep.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״וְכֶסֶף וְזָהָב לֹא יַרְבֶּה לוֹ״, אֶלָּא כְּדֵי לִיתֵּן אַפְסַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the ban on horses to the next ban in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The king may not pile up silver and gold, but he may keep enough to support his army.

steps.title: A ברייתא learns the army exception from 'for himself'
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא asks whether even army money is banned, and answers from 'לוֹ' that only wealth for himself is banned.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: "And silver and gold he shall not greatly accumulate for himself." You might think even enough for the soldiers' upkeep is banned. So the פסוק says "for himself": he may not accumulate for himself, but he may accumulate enough to provide for the soldiers.
steps.whatsHappening: A ברייתא gives the source for the משנה's army exception. It is the same word 'לוֹ' that we saw with horses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא first suggests that all accumulation might be forbidden. It then uses 'לוֹ' to narrow the ban to personal wealth only. This matches what the ברייתא did with horses in Step 10.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
"And silver and gold he shall not greatly accumulate for himself":
one might think even enough to provide the soldiers' upkeep is forbidden?
The פסוק says "for himself":
for himself he may not accumulate,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל מַרְבֶּה הוּא כְּדֵי לִיתֵּן אַפְסַנְיָא.
phrases.english: but he may accumulate enough to provide the soldiers' upkeep.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״וְכֶסֶף וְזָהָב לֹא יַרְבֶּה לוֹ״ – יָכוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source in the פסוק for the משנה's rule in Step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Because of 'לוֹ', only silver and gold for the king's personal use are banned. Money for the army is allowed.

steps.title: Would army money be banned without 'for himself'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks the same question as with horses: did we really need 'לוֹ' to allow money for the army?
steps.simpleTranslation: Is the only reason that the Merciful One wrote "for himself"? Without that, would we have said that even enough for the soldiers' upkeep is also not allowed?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats its challenge from Step 15, this time about silver and gold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It is obvious that a king must pay his soldiers. So it seems strange that a special word would be needed to permit this.

phrases.english: Is the reason that the Merciful One wrote "for himself"?
But if not for this, I would have said:

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ כְּדֵי לִיתֵּן אַפְסַנְיָא נָמֵי לָא?
phrases.english: even enough to provide the soldiers' upkeep is also not allowed?

steps.triggerLanguage: טַעְמָא דִּכְתַב רַחֲמָנָא ״לוֹ״? הָא לָאו הָכִי, הֲוָה אָמֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ברייתא of Step 18 in the same way Step 15 challenged the horses ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's claim that 'לוֹ' is what permits money for the army.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Paying soldiers is obviously allowed, so no word is needed to permit it.

steps.title: 'For himself' allows a generous army budget
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that 'לוֹ' lets the king keep plenty of money for the army, not just the bare minimum.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the word is needed to allow a generous amount.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers just as it did for horses. 'לוֹ' allows extra breathing room in the army budget.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Basic pay for soldiers needs no source. 'לוֹ' adds that the king may keep a comfortable extra amount for the army, since only personal wealth is banned.

keyTerms.meaning: For a generous amount, for breathing room

phrases.english: No, it is needed to allow a generous amount.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 19, using the same idea as Step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframes the word as giving an extra allowance, not the basic permission.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without 'לוֹ', the king could keep only the exact amount needed to pay the soldiers.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because of 'לוֹ', the king may keep a comfortable extra amount for the army.

steps.title: What does 'for himself' teach about wives?
steps.stepSummary: Since 'לוֹ' teaches something about horses and money, the גמרא asks what it teaches in the ban on many wives.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now that you have said that "for himself" is there to teach something, what do you learn from it in "He shall not multiply wives for himself"?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up its final question. If 'לוֹ' always teaches something, what does it teach about wives?
steps.deeperAnalysis: With horses and money, 'לוֹ' meant 'only for personal use, not for the army'. That cannot work for wives, since wives are not for the army. So the גמרא needs a different lesson from 'לוֹ' here.

keyTerms.meaning: For a derivation (to teach a law)
What do you learn from it?

phrases.english: Now that you have said that "for himself" is there to teach something,
"He shall not multiply wives for himself":
what do you learn from it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the idea that 'לוֹ' teaches a lesson (Steps 16 and 20) and applies it to the ban on wives.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What lesson the word 'לוֹ' teaches in the ban on many wives.

steps.title: 'For himself' leaves out ordinary people
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that 'לוֹ' teaches that the ban on many wives applies only to the king, not to ordinary people.
steps.simpleTranslation: It comes to exclude ordinary people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that here 'לוֹ' means 'for him, the king'. So the limit on wives is only for the king.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With wives, 'לוֹ' does not separate personal use from army use. Instead it points to the person: it is the king who is limited, and an ordinary person is not.
steps.whatToRemember: The same word 'לוֹ' teaches two kinds of lessons. With horses and money it allows extra for the army, since only personal use is banned. With wives it shows that the ban is only on the king, not on ordinary people.

phrases.english: To exclude ordinary people.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'לוֹ' in the ban on wives limits the ban to the king and leaves out ordinary people.

steps.title: Two verses give different numbers for שלמה's horse stalls
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה shows that one פסוק says שלמה had forty thousand horse stalls, while another says four thousand.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה pointed out a contradiction. One פסוק says שלמה had forty thousand horse stalls, and another says he had four thousand. How can both be true?
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה puts two פסוקים side by side that seem to disagree about how many horse stalls שלמה had. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both פסוקים use the same phrase, 'stalls of horses,' but the numbers are ten times apart. The question 'הא כיצד' tells us a way of fitting both together is coming.

keyTerms.meaning: Raises a contradiction (literally 'throws' two sources against each other)
How can this be? (asking how to fit both sources together)

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda raises a contradiction:
It is written: "And Shlomo had
forty thousand stalls of horses for his chariots,"
and it is written: "And Shlomo had
four thousand stalls of horses."
How can this be?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After discussing the ban on a מלך having too many horses, the גמרא turns to פסוקים about שלמה's horses.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two פסוקים that count שלמה's horse stalls
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One פסוק says 40,000 and the other says 4,000, so they seem to disagree.

steps.title: Counting buildings and rows makes both numbers true
steps.stepSummary: The answer separates big stable buildings from the rows inside them, so one number counts buildings and the other counts rows in each building.
steps.simpleTranslation: If there were forty thousand stable buildings, each had four thousand rows of horses. And if there were four thousand stable buildings, each had forty thousand rows. Either way, both numbers are true.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה solves his own contradiction. He says one number counts the big stable buildings and the other counts the rows inside each one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key idea is that the two פסוקים are not counting the same thing. One counts buildings and the other counts rows per building, so there is no contradiction. He gives the answer both ways: whichever פסוק counts the buildings, the other counts the rows in each one.

phrases.english: If there were forty thousand stables,
each and every one had in it
four thousand stalls of horses.
And if there were four thousand stables,
each and every one had in it
forty thousand stalls of horses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Each פסוק counts something different: buildings or rows per building
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both numbers seemed to count the same stalls.
steps.terutzMaskana: One number counts buildings and the other counts rows in each building, so both are true.

steps.title: Two verses describe silver differently in שלמה's days
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק shows that one פסוק says silver was worth nothing in שלמה's time, while another compares it to stones.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק pointed out a contradiction. One פסוק says silver was worth nothing in שלמה's days. Another says שלמה made silver in ירושלים like stones.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק sets two פסוקים against each other about how much silver was worth in שלמה's time. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first פסוק says silver had no value at all. The second compares silver to stones, which the גמרא reads as meaning silver still had some value, so the two seem to clash.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak raises a contradiction:
It is written: "Silver was not considered
anything in the days of Shlomo,"
and it is written: "And Shlomo made the silver
in Jerusalem like stones"?
phrases.notes: מלכים א 10:27. For this to clash with the first פסוק, 'stones' must mean something that still has value, like precious stones.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After horses, the גמרא moves to פסוקים about שלמה's silver, which matches the second ban on a מלך: too much money.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two פסוקים describing silver in שלמה's days
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One says silver was worthless, and the other says it was like stones, which means it had some value.

steps.title: Before and after שלמה married בת פרעה
steps.stepSummary: The two פסוקים describe two different times: before שלמה married בת פרעה, and after.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not a problem. One פסוק describes the time before שלמה married בת פרעה, and the other describes the time after he married her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא solves רבי יצחק's contradiction by placing each פסוק in a different period of שלמה's reign.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before the marriage, silver was so plentiful that it was worth nothing. After the marriage, its value went up to 'like stones,' which still meant something. The marriage to בת פרעה marks a turning point downward.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; there is no real problem

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
Here, it was before Shlomo married
phrases.notes: This is the פסוק saying silver was worth nothing.

phrases.english: Pharaoh's daughter;
here, it was after Shlomo married
Pharaoh's daughter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting by time: each פסוק describes a different period
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both פסוקים seemed to describe the same time.
steps.terutzMaskana: Silver was worthless before the marriage to בת פרעה and had some value after it.

steps.title: When שלמה married בת פרעה, the ground for רומי was formed
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק teaches that when שלמה married בת פרעה, גבריאל planted a reed in the sea, and the great city of רומי was later built on the land that formed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק said: When שלמה married בת פרעה, the angel גבריאל came down and stuck a reed into the sea. Sand built up around it, and the great city of רומי was built on it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק adds an אגדה about the same marriage from the last step. He says it planted the seed of רומי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This builds on step 26, where the marriage marked a decline. Here the decline is much bigger. The marriage started the process that created רומי, the empire that would later rule over the Jewish people.

keyTerms.meaning: A sandbank; land that builds up in the water

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how seriously חז"ל viewed שלמה's marriage to בת פרעה. A single wrong step by a great leader can have results that last for generations.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak says:

phrases.aramaic: בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁנָּשָׂא שְׁלֹמֹה אֶת בַּת פַּרְעֹה,
phrases.english: When Shlomo married Pharaoh's daughter,
Gavriel came down and stuck a reed in the sea,
and it brought up a sandbank,
and on it was built the great city of Rome.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁנָּשָׂא שְׁלֹמֹה אֶת בַּת פַּרְעֹה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another teaching from רבי יצחק about the results of שלמה marrying בת פרעה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שלמה's marriage to בת פרעה began the chain of events that led to the rise of רומי.

steps.title: Why doesn't the Torah tell us its reasons?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק asks why the Torah usually does not reveal the reasons behind its מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק also said: Why were the reasons for the Torah's מצוות not revealed?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק asks a question that sets up his next teaching: why the Torah usually hides its reasons.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Most מצוות in the Torah are given without a stated reason. רבי יצחק asks why, and he will answer using שלמה as the example.

keyTerms.meaning: The reasons behind the Torah's מצוות

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yitzchak says:

phrases.aramaic: מִפְּנֵי מָה לֹא נִתְגַּלּוּ טַעֲמֵי תּוֹרָה?
phrases.english: For what reason were the reasons of the Torah not revealed?

steps.triggerLanguage: מִפְּנֵי מָה לֹא נִתְגַּלּוּ טַעֲמֵי תּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third teaching from רבי יצחק about שלמה. This one ties back to the ban on a מלך having many wives.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the Torah does not usually give the reasons for its מצוות.

steps.title: When reasons were revealed, even the greatest man stumbled
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק answers that the Torah gave the reason for two פסוקים, and even the greatest person in the world stumbled because of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because there were two פסוקים whose reasons were revealed, and the greatest person in the world stumbled in them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק answers his own question. When the Torah did reveal reasons, it caused a great person to fail.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Knowing the reason can tempt a person to think, 'The reason does not apply to me, so I may do it.' The 'greatest person in the world' is שלמה, as the next step shows.

keyTerms.meaning: The greatest person in the world

phrases.english: Because two verses had their reasons revealed,
and the greatest person in the world stumbled in them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question asked in step 28.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Revealing reasons led even שלמה to stumble, so the Torah usually hides them.

steps.title: שלמה thought many wives would not turn his heart, but they did
steps.stepSummary: The proof: the Torah says a מלך should not have many wives, so that his heart not turn away. שלמה said he would not turn away, yet in his old age his wives turned his heart.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is written: 'He shall not have many wives.' שלמה said: 'I will have many, and I will not turn away.' And it is written: 'When שלמה was old, his wives turned away his heart.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק proves his point from שלמה and the ban on many wives. שלמה relied on the reason the Torah gave, and in the end he failed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק itself gives the reason: so that his heart not turn away. שלמה thought that if he was careful not to turn away, the ban did not apply to him. The later פסוק shows that the Torah's concern came true anyway.

keyTerms.meaning: Here: I will turn away (from the root סור), not 'forbidden'

steps.confusionAlert: In שלמה's words 'וְלֹא אָסוּר', the word אָסוּר does not mean 'forbidden.' It means 'I will turn away' (from סור). שלמה is saying: 'I will have many wives, but I won't turn away.'
steps.whatToRemember: The Torah usually hides its reasons, because a person might think the reason does not apply to him and break the מצוה. Even שלמה, the wisest of all, fell into this trap with the ban on a מלך having many wives.

phrases.english: It is written: "He shall not have many wives."
phrases.notes: דברים 17:17. That same פסוק goes on to give the reason: so that his heart does not turn away.

phrases.english: Shlomo said:
"I will have many, and I will not turn away."
And it is written: "And it was when Shlomo was old,
his wives turned away his heart."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the example that proves the claim in step 29.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that revealing a מצוה's reason led שלמה to stumble
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברים 17:17 together with מלכים א 11:4: שלמה relied on the stated reason, and his wives still turned his heart.

steps.title: Second proof: שלמה and the horses
steps.stepSummary: The Torah forbids a king from having many horses so he will not send the people back to מצרים. שלמה said he would have many horses and not send anyone back, but in the end chariots came out of מצרים for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is written that a king must not have many horses. שלמה said: I will have many, but I will not bring the people back to Egypt. And it is written that chariots came out of Egypt for six hundred shekels.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second example showing that when the Torah gives a reason, even the wisest person can stumble.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah's reason for the horse limit is to keep the people from going back to מצרים. שלמה thought that since he knew the reason, he could avoid the danger and still have many horses. The פסוק showing chariots coming from מצרים proves the danger came true anyway.

keyTerms.meaning: He shall not get many horses for himself
And I will not bring (the people) back
And so on (the rest of the פסוק)

steps.whatToRemember: Both examples (wives and horses) show the same point: once the Torah reveals the reason, people may think the reason doesn't apply to them, and then they stumble. That is why the Torah usually keeps its reasons hidden.

phrases.english: And it is written: "He shall not accumulate many horses for himself,"
and Shlomo said: "I will accumulate many, and I will not return."
phrases.notes: He means he won't bring the people back to Egypt, which is the reason the פסוק itself gives.

phrases.english: And it is written: "And a chariot went out of Egypt
for six (hundred) etc."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second proof parallel to the wives example in step 30.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יצחק's claim that revealing the reason for a מצוה caused even the greatest person to stumble.
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברים 17:16 together with מלכים א 10:29, showing שלמה's horses led to dealings with מצרים.

steps.title: The king must write his own Torah scroll
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה that a king writes a ספר תורה for himself, and a ברייתא adds that he cannot use his ancestors' scroll for this.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: and he writes a Torah scroll for himself. A ברייתא taught: as long as he does not take pride in his ancestors' scroll.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה about the king and quotes a ברייתא explaining that he must write a new scroll of his own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'for his sake' could have meant he just needs to own a scroll. The ברייתא makes clear that an inherited scroll from his fathers does not count; he must write his own.

phrases.english: "And he writes a Torah scroll for his sake."
phrases.notes: These are words from the משנה, talking about the king.

phrases.english: It was taught: provided that he does not beautify himself
with that of his ancestors.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the אגדה about reasons for מצוות and returns to explain the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A king must write his own ספר תורה and cannot rely on one inherited from his ancestors.

steps.title: Every Jew must write his own scroll, even if he inherited one
steps.stepSummary: רבא teaches that even if a person's parents left him a ספר תורה, it is a מצוה to write his own, based on the פסוק 'write for yourselves this song.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Even if a person's ancestors left him a Torah scroll, it is a מצוה to write one of his own, as it says: 'Now write for yourselves this song.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא teaches that the rule we just saw about the king also applies to every Jew.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא spoke about a king. רבא says the same idea holds for any person: an inherited scroll does not fulfill the מצוה. He learns this from the פסוק that commands each person to write the Torah.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the practical law that every Jew should write (or have written) his own ספר תורה, even if he inherited one.

phrases.english: Rava said:

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהִנִּיחוּ לוֹ אֲבוֹתָיו
phrases.english: Even though his ancestors left him
(that is, a person) a Torah scroll,
it is a מצוה to write one of his own,
as it is stated: "Now write for yourselves this song."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהִנִּיחוּ לוֹ אֲבוֹתָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the king's rule from step 32 to every Jew.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Every person must write his own ספר תורה even if he inherited one.

steps.title: אביי: the rule seems to be only for a king
steps.stepSummary: אביי challenges רבא from a ברייתא that says the king writes his own scroll so he won't rely on others' scrolls. This implies only a king must, not an ordinary person.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי objected: A ברייתא says, 'And he writes for himself a Torah scroll so he won't take pride in others' scrolls.' So a king, yes, but an ordinary person, no!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks רבא's rule by reading the ברייתא closely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא states the 'don't rely on someone else's scroll' rule specifically about the king. If it were true for everyone, why say it about the king? So it seems an ordinary person may use an inherited scroll, against רבא.

phrases.english: Abaye raised an objection to him:
"And he writes for himself a Torah scroll for his sake,
so that he does not beautify himself with that of others."
A king, yes; an ordinary person, no!
phrases.notes: This line isn't in the ברייתא itself; it's אביי's inference from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's rule from step 33.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's rule that every Jew must write his own scroll even if he inherited one.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא states this rule only for a king, implying an ordinary person is exempt.

steps.title: The king's rule is about writing two scrolls
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: the ברייתא is needed to teach that a king writes two scrolls, so it does not imply that an ordinary person is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for two Torah scrolls.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבא by explaining why the ברייתא had to mention the king.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every Jew, including a king, must write one scroll. The ברייתא's special point is that a king writes an extra, second scroll. So it says nothing against ordinary people having to write their own.
steps.confusionAlert: The answer does not say only a king must write a scroll. It says the king writes a second scroll on top of the one every Jew writes.

phrases.english: No, it is needed for two Torah scrolls,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's challenge in step 34.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the purpose of the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא mentions the king because only a king must write his own scroll.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא mentions the king because he writes a second scroll; every Jew still writes one.

steps.title: A ברייתא: the king's two scrolls
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא supports the answer: from the word משנה ('second') we learn the king writes two scrolls, one that goes with him everywhere and one kept in his treasury.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: 'And he shall write for himself a second Torah' — he writes two Torah scrolls for himself: one that goes out and comes in with him, and one placed in his treasury.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to prove that a king writes two scrolls.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word מִשְׁנֵה in the פסוק means 'second' or 'double.' This shows the king has a two-scroll obligation, which explains why the ברייתא spoke about him, and so רבא's rule stands.

keyTerms.meaning: And as it was taught in a ברייתא
Goes out and comes in with him

steps.whatToRemember: Every Jew writes his own ספר תורה, even if he inherited one (רבא). A king writes two: one that always stays with him and one kept in his treasury.

phrases.english: And as it is taught:
"And he shall write for himself a second etc."
phrases.notes: דברים 17:18. Here משנה means 'second,' not the משנה we learn.

phrases.english: he writes for his sake two Torah scrolls:
one that goes out and comes in with him,
and one that is placed for him in his treasury.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 35 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that a king is commanded to write two Torah scrolls.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא on דברים 17:18, reading מִשְׁנֵה as 'second.'

steps.title: The traveling scroll is worn like an amulet
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: the king's scroll that goes everywhere with him is made like an amulet and hung on his arm, based on a פסוק in תהלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The scroll that goes out and comes in with him, he makes like a kind of amulet and hangs it on his arm. As it says: 'I have set ה׳ before me always; because He is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא from the last step keeps going. It explains how the king carries his traveling ספר תורה: he makes it small and wears it on his arm.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 36 said one scroll goes with the king everywhere. This step explains how that works in practice. The פסוק 'I have set ה׳ before me always... at my right hand' hints that the Torah should be with him all the time, right on his arm.

keyTerms.meaning: An amulet, a small object worn on the body
'I have set ה׳ before me always' (תהלים)

phrases.english: The one that goes out and comes in with him,
phrases.notes: This is the first of the king's two scrolls from the previous step, the one that travels with him.

phrases.english: he makes it like a kind of amulet
and hangs it on his arm,
as it is stated: "I have set ה׳ before me always;
for He is at my right hand, I shall not be moved."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא, explaining how the first of the two scrolls is carried.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The king's traveling ספר תורה is made like an amulet and worn on his arm.

steps.title: The scroll may not enter a bathhouse or bathroom
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא adds that the king may not bring this scroll into a bathhouse or a bathroom, because the Torah must be in a place where it is fit to read from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He does not go into the bathhouse or the bathroom with it. As it says: 'And it shall be with him and he shall read from it.' This means it should be in a place where it is fitting to read from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא sets a limit on 'always with him.' The scroll does not come along to places that are unfit for Torah.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא reads the words 'it shall be with him' together with 'he shall read from it.' So the scroll goes with him only to places where reading Torah would be allowed. A bathhouse and a bathroom are not such places.

keyTerms.meaning: A place fit for reading Torah

steps.whatToRemember: The king writes two scrolls. One stays in his treasury. The other is worn on his arm and goes everywhere with him, except places unfit for Torah.

phrases.english: He does not go in with it
not into the bathhouse
and not into the bathroom,
as it is stated: "And it shall be with him and he shall read from it"
meaning, a place that is fit to read from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵינוֹ נִכְנָס בָּהּ לֹא לְבֵית הַמֶּרְחָץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the rule of the previous step: the scroll goes everywhere except unfit places.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The king may not bring his traveling scroll into a bathhouse or bathroom.

steps.title: The Torah's script and language changed in עזרא's time
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא (or מר עוקבא) teaches that the Torah was first given in כתב עברי and לשון הקודש. In עזרא's time it was given again in כתב אשורי and Aramaic. Israel chose כתב אשורי with לשון הקודש.
steps.simpleTranslation: At first, the Torah was given to Israel in כתב עברי and in לשון הקודש. It was given to them again in the days of עזרא in כתב אשורי and in Aramaic. Israel chose for themselves כתב אשורי and לשון הקודש, and left כתב עברי and Aramaic for the commoners.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic connected to writing a ספר תורה: which script and which language the Torah was written in over history.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two separate things are being discussed: the script (the shape of the letters) and the language. The final choice combined the newer script (אשורי) with the original language (לשון הקודש). The older script and Aramaic were left to others.

keyTerms.meaning: The ancient Hebrew script, the older letter shapes
The 'Assyrian' square script, used in a ספר תורה today

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up script and language. 'כתב' is the shape of the letters; 'לשון' is the language. The Torah we use is Hebrew language written in אשורי letters.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר מָר זוּטְרָא, וְאִיתֵּימָא מָר עוּקְבָא:
phrases.english: Mar Zutra said, and some say it was Mar Ukva:
At first, the Torah was given to Israel
in Ivri script and the holy language.
It was given to them again in the days of Ezra
in Ashuri script and the Aramaic language.
Israel chose for themselves
Ashuri script and the holy language,
and they left for the commoners
Ivri script and the Aramaic language.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר זוּטְרָא, וְאִיתֵּימָא מָר עוּקְבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New topic, related to the writing of a ספר תורה discussed before.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The Torah is written in כתב אשורי and לשון הקודש; כתב עברי and Aramaic were left to the commoners.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why a ספר תורה today is written in the square אשורי letters.

steps.title: Who are the commoners?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks who the 'commoners' are, and רב חסדא answers: the כותים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Who are the commoners? רב חסדא said: the כותים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what one word in מר זוטרא's statement means. רב חסדא explains it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מר זוטרא said Israel 'left' the old script and Aramaic for the הדיוטות. רב חסדא tells us these are the כותים, a group who kept using the old script.

phrases.english: Who are the commoners?
Rav Chisda said: The Kutim.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Clarifies a term in the previous statement.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The identity of the 'commoners' mentioned by מר זוטרא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב חסדא: they are the כותים.

steps.title: What is כתב עברי?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what כתב עברי is, and רב חסדא answers: כתב ליבונאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is כתב עברי? רב חסדא said: כתב ליבונאה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a second clarifying question about מר זוטרא's statement, and רב חסדא again explains.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the question is about the old script itself. רב חסדא gives it a name that was known in his time: כתב ליבונאה.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Libona'a script,' the name רב חסדא gives the old Hebrew script

phrases.english: What is Ivri script?
Rav Chisda said: Libona'a script.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second clarifying question on the same statement.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the term כתב עברי refers to.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב חסדא: it is כתב ליבונאה.

steps.title: עזרא was worthy to receive the Torah
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי teaches in a ברייתא that עזרא was great enough for the Torah to be given through him, if משה had not come first.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: רבי יוסי says: עזרא was worthy that the Torah be given to Israel through him, if משה had not come before him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא praising עזרא, since it just mentioned that the Torah was 'given again' in his days.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This explains why the Torah could be 'given again' through עזרא: he was on a level close to משה. Only because משה came first did the original giving go through משה.

keyTerms.meaning: If not for, had it not been

phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Yosei says:
Ezra was worthy
that the Torah be given to Israel through him,
had Moshe not come before him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the mention of עזרא in step 39.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: עזרא was worthy to have the Torah given through him, had משה not preceded him.

steps.title: Proof from the word 'went up'
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי proves his point: the Torah uses 'went up' (עלה) for both משה and עזרא. Just as משה went up for Torah, עזרא's going up was also for Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: About משה it says: 'And משה went up to God.' About עזרא it says: 'This עזרא went up from Babylon.' Just as the going up of משה was for Torah, so the going up of עזרא was for Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי now backs up his claim from the last step by comparing two פסוקים that share the same word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both פסוקים use the word 'עלה' (went up). משה's going up was to receive the Torah. So רבי יוסי learns that עזרא's going up was also connected to Torah, which shows how great he was.
steps.whatToRemember: The Torah is written in כתב אשורי and לשון הקודש, a choice made in עזרא's time. עזרא was so great that the Torah could have been given through him, as shown by the shared word 'went up.'

phrases.english: About Moshe it says:
"And Moshe went up to God,"
About Ezra it says:
"This Ezra went up from Babylon."
Just as the going up stated here was for Torah,
phrases.notes: 'Here' means משה's going up, and 'there' in the next line means עזרא's.

phrases.english: so too, the going up stated there was for Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the scriptural proof for רבי יוסי's claim in step 42.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוסי's claim that עזרא was worthy to receive the Torah.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The shared word עלה in שמות 19:3 and עזרא 7:6.

steps.title: Both משה and עזרא taught Israel statutes and ordinances
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי brings a second parallel. The Torah says משה was commanded to teach חוקים ומשפטים, and the פסוק in עזרא says עזרא set his heart to teach חוק ומשפט in Israel.
steps.simpleTranslation: About משה the פסוק says: 'And ה׳ commanded me at that time to teach you statutes and ordinances.' About עזרא the פסוק says: 'For עזרא set his heart to seek the Torah of ה׳ his God, and to do it, and to teach statutes and ordinances in Israel.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי is adding another proof that עזרא was like משה. Both are described with the same mission: teaching Israel חוקים ומשפטים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 43 the shared word was 'went up' (עלה). Here the shared phrase is about teaching 'statutes and ordinances.' Two matching descriptions make the comparison between משה and עזרא stronger.

keyTerms.meaning: Statutes and ordinances: the laws of the Torah
To seek out, to study deeply

phrases.english: Regarding משה, it says:
"And ה׳ commanded me at that time
to teach you statutes and ordinances."
Regarding עזרא, it says:
"For עזרא had set his heart
to seek the Torah of ה׳ his God
and to do it, and to teach statutes and ordinances in Israel."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second matching description, after the 'went up' comparison in step 43
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוסי's claim that עזרא was fit to have the Torah given through him
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברים 4:14 and עזרא 7:10, which both describe teaching חוקים ומשפטים

steps.title: The Torah's script was changed through עזרא
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי says that even though the Torah was not given through עזרא, the script of the Torah was changed through him. He begins to bring a פסוק as proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: And even though the Torah was not given through him, the script was changed through him, as it says:
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי says what עזרא actually did: he changed the script the Torah is written in. The words 'as it says' set up the proof פסוק, which comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 43-44 showed that עזרא was fit to receive the Torah. Here רבי יוסי admits it did not happen, because משה came first. He still credits עזרא with a real change: the new script. This links back to step 39, where the Torah was given again in כתב אשורי in עזרא's time.

keyTerms.meaning: The script (the letters the Torah is written in)

steps.whyThisMatters: This ties רבי יוסי's praise of עזרא to the topic of the sugya: in which script the Torah is written.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא נִיתְּנָה תּוֹרָה עַל יָדוֹ,
phrases.english: And even though the Torah was not given through him,
the script was changed through him,
as it says:

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא נִיתְּנָה תּוֹרָה עַל יָדוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proofs that עזרא was fit to receive the Torah, this states what he actually accomplished, and sets up a proof פסוק
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even though the Torah was not given through עזרא, the Torah's script was changed through him
